ready1_open_rewrite.raw_question_text:
The following information applies for the next two problems. A circuit has a power source of $\mathcal{E}=5.82 \mathrm{~V}$ connected to three elements in series: an inductor with $L=12.5 \mathrm{mH}$, a capacitor with $C=48.5 \mu \mathrm{F}$, and a diode with threshold voltage $V_{0}=0.65 \mathrm{~V}$. (Of course, the polarity of the diode is aligned with that of the power source.) You close the switch, and after some time, the voltage across the capacitor becomes constant. (Note: An ideal diode with threshold voltage $V_{0}$ is one whose IV characteristic is given by $I=0$ for $V<V_{0}$ and $V=V_{0}$ for $I>0$.)

<image_1>

How much time (in seconds) has elapsed before the voltage across the capacitor becomes constant?

ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: Image description: The diagram shows a single series circuit loop containing a battery/power source, a switch, an inductor labeled L, a capacitor labeled C, and a diode oriented consistently with the battery polarity. Thus the elements are in series and the diode is forward biased while current flows. Reasoning: While the diode conducts, model it as a constant voltage drop V0. Kirchhoff's loop law gives L dI/dt + q/C + V0 = E, with I = dq/dt. Therefore L q'' + q/C = E - V0. Initially, just after the switch is closed, q(0) = 0 and I(0) = 0. The driven LC solution is q(t) = C(E - V0)[1 - cos(t/sqrt(LC))]. Hence I(t) = dq/dt = C(E - V0)(1/sqrt(LC)) sin(t/sqrt(LC)). The capacitor voltage becomes constant when the current first returns to zero and the diode stops conducting. The first nonzero time satisfying sin(t/sqrt(LC)) = 0 is t = pi sqrt(LC). Substituting L = 12.5 mH = 12.5e-3 H and C = 48.5 microF = 48.5e-6 F gives t = pi sqrt((12.5e-3)(48.5e-6)) = 2.446e-3 s.

method.method_draft: Read the circuit as a single series loop: battery, inductor, capacitor, and forward-biased threshold diode. While current flows, replace the diode by a constant voltage drop V0, so Kirchhoff's law gives L dI/dt + q/C + V0 = E with I = dq/dt, or L q'' + q/C = E - V0. Use initial conditions just after closing the switch: q(0)=0 and I(0)=0. Solve the driven LC equation: q(t)=C(E−V0)[1−cos(t/sqrt(LC))], so I(t)=C(E−V0)(1/sqrt(LC)) sin(t/sqrt(LC)). The capacitor voltage becomes constant when the current first falls to zero and the diode stops conducting, i.e. at sin(t/sqrt(LC))=0 for the first nonzero time: t=pi sqrt(LC). Substitute L=12.5 mH and C=48.5 microF to get t=pi sqrt(12.5e-3*48.5e-6)=2.446e-3 s.

method.method_draft: Treat the conducting interval as an undamped LC oscillator about a shifted equilibrium rather than solving the full step-response explicitly. From the diagram/text, the diode is forward biased initially, so while it conducts the battery effectively supplies a constant net voltage E−V0 to the LC pair. Define the shifted capacitor voltage x = Vc − (E−V0). The LC dynamics are simple harmonic with angular frequency omega=1/sqrt(LC). Initially Vc=0 and I=0, so x=−(E−V0) and the oscillator starts at a turning point in phase space. The capacitor voltage becomes fixed when the current next reaches zero; that is the opposite turning point of the LC oscillation, reached after half a period: t=T/2=pi/omega=pi sqrt(LC). At that instant the LC would try to reverse current, but the diode blocks, leaving the capacitor voltage constant. Insert L=12.5e-3 H and C=48.5e-6 F to obtain 2.446e-3 s.
